articles.title: Elderly Devon woman too scared to turn heating on as costs soar
articles.summary: Roslynn Garner-Gatley starts using a hot water bottle, bed socks and earlier bedtimes to stay warm.
articles.body:
A woman has said she is frightened to put her heating on because the cost of domestic oil has nearly doubled.

Roslynn Garner-Gatley, 76, lives in a three-bedroom semi-detached cottage in Yealmpton, south Devon, with no gas supply and relies entirely on oil for heating and hot water.

She said her oil tank held 1,000 litres (220 gallons). About six months earlier, she bought 500 litres (110 gallons) for £317 plus VAT but, when she contacted her supplier for a current quote, she was told the same amount would cost £600 plus VAT.

Garner-Gatley said: "I did not expect at my age after working for 50 years to be in a situation where I am terrified of putting on the heating because of the price of it."

Garner-Gatley said she had started going to bed earlier to keep warm while watching television and had recently begun using a hot water bottle and bed socks as evening temperatures dropped.

She said instead of keeping hot water on a timer, she only switched it on when she needed it for washing, cooking or bathing before turning it off again.

She added that people living in rural areas who depended on oil had "no choice" but to buy it.

She said: "After working all my life I didn't expect to be constantly worrying about how to keep warm at my age. It is really quite frightening."

Heating fuel costs have risen by up to 82% since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, according to Minster for Energy Consumers Polly Billington.

Earlier in October, the government promised better regulation of the sector .

Ministers said they would tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things went wrong.

Minimum order levels set for some customers would also be reviewed, they added.

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, said: "We have pledged £53m in support for vulnerable households on heating oil, while helping people switch to clean heat with Boiler Upgrade Scheme grants worth £9,000.

"We are also reforming the heating oil sector, holding suppliers to account and giving consumers confidence that they will get a fair deal."

Cornwall Council and Devon County Council have money available for households struggling with increasing heating oil costs from their crisis resilience funds, which are provided by the government.

Cornwall Council said it had issued payments of £300 to 1,386 households, a total spend of £415,800, which would double after a decision was made to award a further £300 to the same households.

The Devon fund, worth about £8.4m a year, is available through district councils, and is targeted at low‑income households facing an "essential cost they cannot afford".

Plymouth City Council and Torbay Council also have their own crisis resilience funds.

articles.title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
articles.summary: Disaffection has often driven down turnout among Arab Israelis, but there is a strong push to get rid of the right-wing governing coalition.
articles.body:
At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.

Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.

"I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."

Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.

If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.

A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.

Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority.

"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."

Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending.

There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis.

Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank.

How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?

The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity. Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government".

To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders.

At Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party.

I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties.

"In a word it's racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel."

Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings.

These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas.

While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.

Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc.

For this election, he has taken the surprise step of giving the number two position on his slate to a Jewish former police official and centrist member of parliament, Yoav Segalovitz. Abbas believes Eisenkot and others will be more open to an alliance with his party after the election and insists he wants to join the next government.

"We've reached the conclusion that parliamentary representation is not enough to serve Arab society. We decided to take responsibility, to become part of the solution to our problems and to offer hope to both Arabs and Jews," he tells me.

"That's why our approach has been driven by a desire to reach a position of influence, not merely representation."

Meanwhile, the Joint List - which is made up of secular parties and advocates for equal rights for Arab Israelis, an end to Israeli military occupation of Palestinian territories, and a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict - aims to wield a position of influence within the opposition.

It talks of providing an electoral "safety net" to those who could replace the Netanyahu government, in return for support on important policies.

A main issue in this election for Arab Israelis is rampant gang crime.

In September, a poll by the Israel Democracy Institute think tank found that this was the most important factor for 53.5% of Arab citizens when deciding which party to vote for.

Murders within the community reached a record high of 252 last year – about five times higher than the number of Jewish Israelis who were killed, according to the Abraham Initiatives, a Jewish-Arab organisation that promotes coexistence.

In Jaffa, a mixed Arab-Jewish neighbourhood which is now joined to Tel Aviv, Ziad Samouni shows me where his son, Hussein, was shot dead by two gunmen on a motorcycle near his home last November.

No arrests have been made in his case. With a low percentage of cases solved, Arab-Israelis accuse the government of inaction.

"It seems they're interested in making sure we reach a situation where the killer is never caught, allowing Arabs in Arab society to keep killing one another," says Samouni, who is now part of a support group, Israeli-Palestinian Bereaved Families for Peace.

The Israeli police told the BBC its investigation into Hussein's murder remained active, adding that it took "every case of violence and crime with the utmost seriousness."

"As a father who's lost a son, of course, I want this bloodshed to end," Samouni tells me. "I wish every Arab citizen who believes there needs to be a change sees that this is a time to go to vote."

This month, Israel's Supreme Court overruled a decision by the Central Elections Committee to disqualify the United Arab List and the Joint List as well as two of their members.

The committee, which is dominated by the governing coalition, argued that they broke a law banning candidates who deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish state. The parties and their representatives strongly denied it.

With just days to go before voting, back in Nazareth, some motorists display flags for their preferred party on their cars.

The stakes are high in this election: Arab citizens could yet decide who wields power in Israel, and they also see this vote as key to their own future in the country.

articles.title: Happy Mondays boosted by Oasis return, says Bez ahead of Keele show
articles.summary: The maracas player spoke of his love of touring, ahead of the band's upcoming show in Staffordshire.
articles.body:
Happy Mondays star Bez says the band have been boosted by the "incredible" long-awaited comeback of Oasis.

The maracas player, real name Mark Berry, said the return of the Britpop legends shone a renewed light on the Manchester music scene and the artists it spawned.

The 62-year-old toured with his Happy Mondays bandmates in March and April to celebrate 35 years since the release of album Pills 'n' Thrills and Bellyaches.

The group are scheduled to play two more UK shows this year, including in Keele, Staffordshire, on 13 November.

Speaking to BBC Radio Stoke ahead of the gig, Bez said: "We're lucky enough to be part of that Manchester scene which, at the time, grew so big it was unbelievable.

"We've got that legendary status from that time, and of course Oasis coming back last year helped all things Manchester again, so I think that's given us a push as well."

Liam and Noel Gallagher announced the return of Oasis in 2024 before they reunited on stage in July 2025 – the first time they had performed together since 2009.

"It's absolutely incredible, the phenomenon of Oasis," Bez said.

"I was actually blown away by it all, both to see them at Heaton Park and to see hordes of young people all running around. It was just an incredible moment."

Happy Mondays were formed in Salford in 1980, with Bez joining as a dancer and maracas player in 1986.

They saw commercial success in the late 1980s and early 1990s, with their hits including Step On and Kinky Afro.

Bez said the members knew each other when they were growing up and described them as a "schoolboy band".

"It's so great because it's so rare these days that you get that," he added.

"The most amazing thing about it all is, when we did actually set off, we were all so naive in music because, these days, people go to college or sixth form.

"You're forced into some sort of education and a lot of people choose to go to music college and learn the basics of music.

"When we set off, we didn't even know what one-two-three-four time was."

Bez said he still loved gigging and the "comradeship" which came with the bandmates being together.

Nowadays he is also accompanied on the road by his wife, Firouzeh, who joined the group as a singer.

He said: "It's nice to share the bedroom with somebody and get a cuddle – you can't beat that early-morning cuddle."

Bez has also appeared on popular Channel 4 show Celebrity Gogglebox with his bandmate Shaun Ryder.

He remembered filming episodes during the Covid-19 pandemic and the social distancing rules which were in force at the time.

"We [Shaun and I] were looking at each other going 'do you know what germs we've shared over the years?'. We've been in a band for 40 years together."

Bez described the programme as a "great show" and revealed how they would be "plied" with drinks during filming sessions.

"Obviously after a few Jamesons and Guinnesses you get quite loose-tongued," he added. "Some of our observations can't be used on television as we get carried away."

Happy Mondays will be performing at the Keele University Students' Union in Keele, Staffordshire, on 13 November.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Social media influencer Amir Shokeen has apologised after a video purportedly showing him subjecting a youth from Tripura to racial abuse and humiliation triggered widespread condemnation, even as the Delhi Police’s Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit is set to investigate the viral clip.In an apology video, Shokeen said he had intended the video as a joke and sought forgiveness from the people of Tripura and chief minister Manik Saha, who had called for action over the incident.“Jai Babaji, brothers, as you know, I made a video, it was a joke video, but for that, if any of the brothers of Tripura are offended, I am apologizing again, forgive me,” he said.Referring to Saha’s post on the controversy, Shokeen added that he was apologising to the chief minister as well. “I made a mistake,” he said, claiming that he had deleted the video and was seeking forgiveness with folded hands.“I have made more than 2,000 videos, but no one has ever hurt anyone, and Hindus, Muslims, all the community, I have never done anything wrong with anyone,” he said.In another video posted on Instagram, Shokeen claimed that the video was scripted.The apology comes amid growing demands for action over the video, which allegedly showed the influencer directing racial slurs and abusive remarks at a youth from Tripura, referring to him as “Chinese” and humiliating him in public.Delhi Police’s IFSO unit to investigate viral videoThe Delhi Police’s Special Police Unit for North Eastern Region (SPUNER) has formally written to the IFSO unit, asking it to investigate the viral video, officials said on Thursday.The Tripura Students Forum Delhi (TSFD), in a complaint dated October 21 addressed to the joint commissioner of police, SPUNER, sought an urgent and impartial investigation into the incident.The forum alleged that the video depicted a person from Tripura being subjected to sexual assault, harassment and humiliating treatment by a social media content creator.The complaint identified the Instagram account @amirshoksen as allegedly linked to the incident and sought verification of the identity and role of the person operating it, as well as others who may have participated in or recorded the alleged incident.The forum also urged police to preserve electronic evidence, including the original recording, metadata, account details and upload history, and take steps to prevent further harassment or intimidation of the youth.It sought registration of an FIR wherever warranted by the facts and applicable legal provisions.Kiren Rijiju, Manik Saha demand actionThe video has drawn condemnation from political leaders, including Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju and Tripura chief minister Manik Saha.Rijiju said the accused would face action, asserting that Delhi and Tripura Police would take the matter forward.“This evil man will be punished. There was a delay in lodging the official complaint, but Delhi Police and Tripura Police will teach him a hard lesson,” the minister said in a post on X.Saha had earlier directed the state’s director general of police to coordinate with Delhi Police over the incident. Leaders across party lines in Tripura have also condemned the alleged conduct and demanded legal action.The IFSO unit is examining the matter. articles.title: Mariska Hargitay helped fund Detroit’s effort to test abandoned sexual assault kits; by April 2025, the wider project had secured 263 convictions as investigations continued across decades
articles.summary: More than 250 convictions have emerged from a long-running investigation into thousands of sexual assault cases in Detroit, Michigan, where evidence had
articles.body: More than 250 convictions have emerged from a long-running investigation into thousands of sexual assault cases in Detroit, Michigan, where evidence had remained untested for decades. American actress Mariska Hargitay, best known for her role as detective Olivia Benson in Law & Order: SVU, was among those who helped fund and support the effort. According to the Wayne County Prosecutor's Office, the Detroit Sexual Assault Kit Project had secured 263 convictions by April 2025, while investigations and prosecutions were still continuing.The project began in 2009, when authorities discovered 11,341 sexual assault evidence kits inside a Detroit Police Department warehouse. According toAccording to Wayne County, Michigan, the kits related to cases dating from 1984 to 2009, but none had been submitted for testing. The discovery meant that evidence collected over 25 years was still awaiting examination.Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy took responsibility for addressing the backlog. However, examining such a large number of kits required considerable funding, which was difficult to secure at the time. Detroit was facing serious financial problems, and the county administration did not initially provide the money needed for the project.Worthy began approaching organisations and private donors for assistance. What followed was a fundraising effort involving government agencies, charitable foundations and individuals from across the United States and abroad. Hargitay's Joyful Heart Foundation eventually became one of the organisations supporting the initiative.How Hargitay became involved in the investigationHargitay had already been working with survivors of sexual assault through the Joyful Heart Foundation when she met Worthy at a congressional hearing in 2010. Their meeting marked the beginning of the foundation's involvement in Detroit's effort to examine the abandoned evidence.Her contribution was not limited to financial support. Hargitay also helped draw attention to the issue among lawmakers, using her public profile to support Worthy's campaign for changes in the handling of sexual assault evidence.In a 2024 interview featured on the Dateline: True Crime Weekly podcast, Worthy recalled asking Hargitay to come to Detroit after they had appeared before lawmakers. "She said she would, and she did," Worthy said.The actress subsequently attended a breakfast organised for legislators whom Worthy had struggled to reach. According to the prosecutor, Hargitay's presence helped bring attention to the issue and encouraged political support for reforms. "And I am telling you, that legislation that helped us crack this problem in Michigan sailed through," Worthy recalled.Why testing the evidence took yearsOne of the biggest challenges was the cost of examining the evidence. According to the Los Angeles Times, which reported on the podcast in August 2024, testing a single kit could cost between $1,200 and $1,500. With 11,341 kits awaiting examination, the authorities needed millions of dollars.Funding eventually came from several sources, including the federal government, Michigan authorities, Wayne County and private organisations. Donations were also received from people in all 50 US states and nine foreign countries.The work went beyond examining evidence already held by police. Investigators also had to follow up on findings from cases that were sometimes decades old.The results showed how serious the consequences of leaving evidence untested could be. In one case highlighted by the Wayne County Prosecutor's Office, evidence from a 2002 sexual assault was linked to a man who had later been imprisoned for three murders committed during the following seven years.By the project's tenth anniversary in 2019, according to the prosecutor's office, testing of all 11,341 kits had been completed.Cases reached far beyond DetroitThe investigation eventually extended well beyond Michigan. By April 2025, cases connected to the Detroit project had been linked to 40 US states, including California, Texas, New York, Florida and Washington.The Los Angeles Times reported that the effort had helped solve more than 5,000 cases and identify 22 serial rapists, citing information shared through NBC's coverage of the project.The work also contributed to changes in how Michigan handles sexual assault evidence. The state introduced legislation establishing timelines for submitting kits for testing, along with a tracking system that allows survivors to follow the progress of DNA testing.Hargitay later helped bring the issue to television audiences through I Am Evidence, a 2018 documentary she produced. The film examined the problem of untested sexual assault kits and featured Worthy's efforts in Detroit. It received an Emmy Award in 2019.Investigations continue despite completion of testingAlthough the original kits have been tested, the cases connected to them have not all reached a conclusion. The Wayne County Prosecutor's Office said investigations and prosecutions were continuing in 2025, more than 15 years after the evidence was discovered.Worthy has remained associated with Hargitay's foundation, serving as its vice-chair and co-chair of its National Council of Leadership and Innovation.The Detroit project has also been used to develop practices for investigating sexual assault cases and managing evidence in other parts of the United States.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2004, Florida researchers used 36 recycled oyster shells per reef mat, helping restore Mosquito Lagoon reefs to around 1,000 live oysters per square metre
articles.summary: In Florida’s Mosquito Lagoon, the return of oyster reefs began with a relatively simple idea: give young oysters somewhere stable to settle.
articles.body: In Florida’s Mosquito Lagoon, the return of oyster reefs began with a relatively simple idea: give young oysters somewhere stable to settle. In 2004, researchers started testing small mats fitted with recycled oyster shells, placing them in areas where boat traffic had damaged existing reefs. Each mat carried 36 shells, held in place by plastic ties and arranged on a mesh base. The approach was designed to recreate the structure of a natural reef in parts of the lagoon where oysters struggled to survive. According to the study published in Sustainability by MDPI titled, ‘The Use of Non-Plastic Materials for Oyster Reef and Shoreline Restoration: Understanding What Is Needed and Where the Field Is Headed’, over the following years, the restored areas developed into productive oyster habitat, with average densities reaching around 1,000 live oysters per square metre. The results also raised questions about the materials used to achieve that recovery.Mosquito Lagoon oyster reef decline and the need for restorationMosquito Lagoon lies along Florida’s east coast, forming the northernmost section of the Indian River Lagoon system. Its shallow waters support coastal habitats that provide shelter for fish and invertebrates, filter water and help protect shorelines from wave action. Oyster reefs are part of that system, but large areas of the lagoon’s oyster habitat had been lost over several decades.Reportedly, between 1943 and 2009, oyster acreage in Mosquito Lagoon declined by more than 40%, according to research cited in the restoration assessment. Several pressures have contributed to oyster declines across the southeastern United States, including disease, harmful algal blooms, changes in freshwater flows and human activity along the coast. In this part of Florida, recreational boating presented a particular problem.Waves generated by passing boats could dislodge oyster clusters and push them beyond the intertidal zone, where conditions became unsuitable for their survival. The damage was especially relevant in the shallow lagoon, where natural oyster recruitment remained strong in areas away from heavily used boating channels.Oyster reef restoration mats use 36 recycled shells to support oyster growthResearchers began developing oyster restoration mats in 2004, using a design intended to resemble the low profile of existing patch reefs. Each unit covered 0.25 square metres and consisted of industrial aquaculture mesh made from extruded polyethylene. Thirty-six recycled oyster shells were attached to each mat using plastic cable ties threaded through holes drilled near the hinge, or umbo, of each shell.The mats were positioned across the historic reef footprint at the appropriate intertidal elevation. Workers connected the individual units in a quilt-like arrangement, using cement rings and cable ties to help keep them in place. Rather than relying on loose shells that could be shifted by waves, the design provided a more stable foundation for oyster larvae to settle on and develop.Mosquito Lagoon oyster reef restoration reaches 1,000 oysters per square metreWithin three to eight years of deployment, the restored reefs averaged about 1,000 live oysters per square metre, according to the research cited in the assessment. Those densities met or exceeded the levels recorded on intact natural reefs in the same local environment.The findings suggested that a relatively low-profile structure could help restore oyster habitat when placed in suitable conditions. The researchers were not attempting to build a completely artificial reef from scratch. Instead, they were providing a stable base in areas where oysters had historically occurred but where disturbance had made it harder for reef structure to persist.Plastic pollution concerns drive a shift in oyster reef restoration materialsThe original mats achieved their intended purpose, but their construction relied on plastic mesh and cable ties. As concern about plastic pollution in marine environments grew, restoration practitioners began looking more closely at the materials being left in coastal waters.Microplastics have been documented across marine environments, including estuaries, and have been detected in many species. Filter-feeding animals such as oysters are of particular interest because they draw water through their bodies while feeding. The research assessment does not establish that the Mosquito Lagoon restoration mats caused increased microplastic pollution, but it describes a wider concern that adding plastic structures to marine environments could contribute to an existing problem.Removing plastic from a restoration project is not as straightforward as replacing one material with another. A substitute needs to provide enough structural support during installation and remain stable while oysters settle and grow. The Mosquito Lagoon team therefore sought to retain the basic mat design while changing the materials used to construct it. The aim was to preserve the conditions that had helped oysters establish themselves without relying on conventional plastic mesh and ties.Biodegradable oyster reef mats support growth while reducing plastic useThe replacement approach used BESE-elements®, a biodegradable lattice made from potato starch, with stainless-steel wire used instead of plastic cable ties. The material was intended to provide a plastic-free alternative to the original mesh-based mats while maintaining a similar restoration method.Monitoring of the new mats in Mosquito Lagoon found that oyster recruitment was not significantly different from recruitment on the earlier plastic mats after one or two years. By the end of the second year, the biodegradable mats supported an average of 676.4 live oysters per square metre. That was a substantial population, although it was a different measure and timeframe from the average density of around 1,000 oysters per square metre recorded on the earlier restored reefs within three to eight years.The assessment also recorded relatively little physical damage. Of 500 mats deployed on reefs, eight were damaged by wave energy where protective shell bags had not been placed beyond the edges. The material did lose some mass during its first year in the water, with estimates suggesting a half-life of 4.4 to 6.7 years. That raised a longer-term question: whether the structures would remain intact long enough to support reef development under different environmental conditions.Florida expands oyster reef restoration with alternatives to plastic materialsThe experience in Mosquito Lagoon forms part of a broader shift in Florida, where restoration teams have been testing alternatives to plastic in oyster reefs and living shorelines. Options include natural fibres, cement-based structures, metal mesh, recycled shell and rock. Each has different practical advantages, and the most suitable choice can depend on the scale of a project and the conditions at the site.A statewide assessment of restoration practitioners found that projects using non-plastic materials were being carried out in a range of settings, from small community efforts to larger shoreline works. Many respondents reported that the materials performed as well as or better than expected, and 86% said they were willing to use non-plastic options again or recommend them to colleagues.You use AI every day. articles.title: After retiring and moving to Phoenix in the early 1950s, Grover Thompson spent 22 years building a rock garden filled with hundreds of figures, miniature buildings, windmills and fountains
articles.summary: Explore the fascinating journey of Grover Thompson, who transformed his retirement into a vibrant rock garden filled with hundreds of whimsical figures, miniature buildings, and fountains in Phoenix. Discover the history and preservation efforts of this folk art site.
articles.body: Sunnyslope is a mountainside neighborhood in north Phoenix. On one residential street, the front yard of a private home is filled with windmills topped with colorful mosaics, small concrete figures and rock fountains. Phoenix New Times notes that much of it can be seen from the street. The garden is the work of Grover Cleveland Thompson, a retired heavy-equipment operator who built it over two decades. It is a private property and not a public park, yet it has a long record of visitors, advocates and local attention.Thompson’s retirement to Sunnyslope in 1952 The SPACES Archives entry Sunnyslope Rock Garden, written by Jo Farb Hernández, says Thompson retired and moved to the neighborhood in 1952. He began a massive environment of rocks and concrete, ornamented with natural and man-made found objects and worked on it for 22 years. The entry says he was inspired by Petersen Rock Garden in Bend, Oregon, near where he used to live. The Minnesota Museum of the Mississippi page Sunnyslope Rock Garden, Phoenix, Arizona places the move around 1953, when Thompson and his second wife, Nancy, bought a patch of undeveloped land in Sunnyslope. Sources therefore differ by a year on his arrival.Fiestaware shards and Halloween-mask faces as inexpensive materialsThe above-mentioned SPACES entry states that most of the characters are painted in bright colors since Thompson used pieces of Fiestaware for their cheap decoration. The entry further claims that many of the faces were created using the old Halloween masks as molds. The Phoenix New Times confirms the information about the masks, stating that he poured concrete into the Halloween masks from the 1950s and lists pottery, broken bottles, glass pieces, clay and rocks among the materials used. According to ABC15, Julia Taggart of the Sunnyslope Historical Society claims that the neighbors used to leave pottery and china outside his mailbox and he would use them in his garden the next day.Seven fountains and seven windmills reported by Phoenix New TimesOver 22 years, Thompson constructed seven fountains, seven windmills and a model of the Seattle Space Needle, Phoenix New Times reports. At its peak, SPACES says, the garden contained several hundred figures, miniature buildings, windmills and fountains, while Roadside America gives a more modest tally of over 50 mosaic-clad structures, including Dutch windmills, a ziggurat, a wishing well and a miniature cliffside pueblo. Sources also disagree on the height of the Space Needle replica, which Roadside America puts at nine feet and a 2002 Phoenix New Times feature at 12 feet. Even so, all sources agree about the nature of the garden, a crowded miniature landscape of buildings and cultural icons.Work stopped in 1974 as Thompson’s health failedPhoenix New Times explains that the expansion stopped in 1974 due to Thompson's failing health. He died in the late 1970s, with the museum site giving the fall of 1977 and SPACES giving 1978. The museum site adds that the garden would probably have been forgotten after his death but for a stroke of luck that led to its sale.Marion Blake’s purchase in 1979 According to SPACES, the house was purchased in 1979 by Marion Blake, who is a native of New York. The museum states that Blake obtained the house and garden from Cloydene, Thompson’s daughter, on the condition that she keep it safe and she went on to care for it for more than four decades. She made sure that cracks in the cement were fixed and that the delicate sculptures were preserved during storms.The City of Phoenix staff report Phoenix City Staff Report Z-94-24-3, dated September 6, 2024, requests Historic Preservation overlay zoning for the Thompson Rock Garden. The report states that the property was first identified in the 1979 Phoenix Historic Building Survey and that the Historic Preservation Commission began the designation process on June 17, 2024. It also describes the garden as one of only two folk art sites in Phoenix, the other being the Louis Lee Rock Garden.The commission adopted its recommendation at its September 16, 2024 meeting, as its results notice shows and Phoenix approved the overlay zoning in December 2024, which the museum page says made the garden a designated historic site. ABC15 reports that more than 300 people supported the decision.Visiting the garden todaySPACES states that the garden is usually open to visitors on the first Friday of each month and that parts of it can be seen from beyond the perimeter fence, a description the museum webpage echoes. Since it is private property, visitors are encouraged to check the opening times beforehand.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?
articles.summary: Many view it as one of the most pivotal elections in Israel's history, with global implications.
articles.body:
Israel's general election takes place on Tuesday 27 October.

It's the first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel and its subsequent conflicts in Gaza and with Iran, Hezbollah and the Houthis.

Many view it as one of the most pivotal elections in Israel's history, with global implications.

Current polling puts incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, to become prime minister.

Eisenkot's popularity stems partly from his military credentials and his relative newness in politics, having formed his Yashar Party only last year.

He lost his son, a soldier, in the first months of the Gaza war, and served in Israel's war cabinet under Netanyahu until resigning in 2024 over disagreements about the conflict. He has built his campaign on calls for accountability over the security failures that led to 7 October.

Other opposition leaders include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security and advocate permanent Israeli control over much of the occupied West Bank - and Yair Golan, a left-winger who supports Israel's withdrawal from large parts of the territory. Despite their differences, they could work with Eisenkot to form a government.

Netanyahu's current government is the most right-wing in Israel's history. In order to remain in power, he will likely have to rely on the support of some of his existing far-right coalition partners. Some hold ultra-nationalist positions, such as calling for Israel to annex the West Bank and for the "migration" of Palestinians from Gaza - which could amount to the forced displacement of civilians. Some members of Netanyahu's own Likud party have also called for Palestinian "migration" from the territory.

There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.

Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters

Israel's parliament - known as the Knesset - has 120 seats, meaning a government must hold 61 seats to command a majority.

Israel uses a proportional representation voting system, meaning governments have always been coalitions of multiple parties.

This means that after election day, it may take weeks or even months before the next government is formed - with different parties wrangling for concessions and deals being struck.

If no bloc can form a majority, it is possible a minority government could take power.

The dominating topic has been security - with the challengers to Netanyahu all heavily criticising the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken back to Gaza as hostages. Nevertheless, Netanyahu has once again framed himself as "Mr Security", pointing to strategic victories in Israel's wars since 2023.

Conscription is also a major topic. Historically, ultra-Orthodox Jewish men in full-time religious study have been exempt from military service, but since war broke out this has become an increasingly divisive policy.

Judicial reform has also featured heavily during the campaign. Netanyahu's government is still pursuing contentious plans for reforms to the judicial system, which led to mass protests before 7 October. Critics say the plans would compromise the independence of the judiciary and threaten democracy.

As in many countries, cost of living is another key issue. Food and housing costs have grown steadily in recent years.

What does it mean for Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank?

A year on from the ceasefire in Gaza, Israel continues to carry out near-daily strikes on the territory - saying it is targeting Hamas operatives - and maintains control of more than half of it.

More than 74,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza since 7 October 2023, according to the Hamas-run health ministry - whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

In the West Bank, attacks by Jewish settlers are at an all-time high, according to UN records, while Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law, are rapidly expanding.

So for Palestinians, the shape of Israel's government is a major factor in their lives.

On Gaza, the two leading camps - headed by Netanyahu and Eisenkot - hold similar positions - with both supporting Donald Trump's peace plan, which would see Hamas give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the territory. Eisenkot recently pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through military means if necessary.

In the West Bank, Netanyahu's camp largely wants to continue with its policy of settlement expansion.

Eisenkot supports Israeli settlements in general, but opposes proceeding with the controversial E1 settlement project which would, in effect, split the West Bank in two. He also wants to close some unauthorised settler outposts built on Palestinian land, create conditions for a final peace settlement with the Palestinians, and crack down on extremist Jewish settlers.

For decades, many mainstream Israeli politicians advocated for a two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - although Netanyahu has long opposed it. But support for the idea has been declining for years. In this election, none of the leading Jewish parties are campaigning on it, and many have outright rejected it.

How Israel is expanding settlements in drive to reshape West Bank

At 22:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on election day, Israeli broadcasters will publish exit polls. These will give some indication of the direction of voting, but can vary significantly and current polling suggests a clear projected winner is unlikely.

Preliminary results are expected the next day, with official results scheduled to be published on 4 November.

After consulting with party leaders, President Isaac Herzog will then invite whichever leader he believes has the best chance of forming a government to do so.

This process can take more than a month, and if it fails the president may ask another leader to try. If that also fails, Knesset members can ask the president to allow a third leader to try. And if that fails, new elections will be called.

Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as parties struggled time and again to co-operate.

articles.title: Married at First Sight Australia: Police investigate show after 'inappropriate' allegations
articles.summary: New South Wales Police say inquiries took place "following a report of inappropriate content being shared".
articles.body:
Married at First Sight Australia is facing fresh controversy after police launched an investigation into the hit reality TV show.

New South Wales told BBC News that inquiries had taken place "following a report of inappropriate content being shared".

Channel Nine, which broadcasts Married at First Sight Australia, confirmed that it was "aware of a police investigation" involving the show's production company.

It is the latest blow for the show, after a BBC News investigation earlier this year into MAFS Australia revealed cast members said they had not been told their partners had previous drug and violence convictions.

Those revelations led to a warning from Australia's media watchdog, which called them "serious and disturbing".

The British version of Married at First Sight, known to many as MAFS UK, was separately plunged into crisis in May after BBC Panorama reported rape allegations from two female cast members - allegations the men involved have denied.

MAFS UK is made by a different production company to the Australian version.

Married at First Sight shows single people agreeing to "marry" total strangers after meeting for the first time at their mock weddings.

The marriages are not legally binding, but viewers see the couples go on "honeymoons", before moving in together and navigating their relationships - all while being filmed, almost every day.

According to industry news website TV Blackbox , a male cast member on the current series of MAFS Australia made a formal complaint to the police after producers allegedly shared private information about him with his on-screen bride.

Married at First Sight Australia stars not told partners had drug and violence convictions

Married at First Sight Australia allegations 'disturbing', says country's watchdog

Married at First Sight UK brides tell BBC they were raped by on-screen husbands

A spokesperson for New South Wales Police Force told BBC News: "On Monday 24 August 2026, officers attached to South Sydney Police Area Command commenced an investigation following a report of inappropriate content being shared.

"Following inquiries, the matter will be referred to WA [Western Australia] Police Force."

BBC News has approached WA Police Force, who said the referral has not yet been received.

A spokesperson for Channel Nine said: "We are aware of a police investigation involving Endemol Shine Australia and all enquiries should be directed to them."

Endemol Shine Australia, which makes MAFS Australia, has not responded to multiple requests for comment over the latest developments.

In June, a BBC News investigation heard from nine former cast members from MAFS Australia, who urged the show to improve its background checks and to stop allowing individuals with previous convictions or allegations on the show.

One woman from last year's Australian series told us she was not told the man she had been matched with had a previous drug conviction and only found out after the show ended. "There should be informed consent," she told us.

Responding to those claims at the time, Channel 9 and Endemol Shine Australia said they had "strong protocols in place to ensure participant safety and wellbeing".

As well as being a huge hit in Australia, the show is popular in the UK and is shown on Channel 4.

The broadcaster pulled all the UK episodes of MAFS from its streaming service just hours ahead of the transmission of the Panorama investigation in May, but MAFS Australia remains available to watch.

In July, BBC News revealed that a cast member from MAFS UK had been arrested on suspicion of rape following the Panorama programme.

The individual is not being named; nor is the alleged victim. Anyone who makes an allegation of rape is entitled to anonymity by law.

The media regulator Ofcom has also launched an official investigation into the hit Channel 4 show.

The UK version, which has been running for 10 seasons, is one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.

The broadcaster has commissioned a review into contributor welfare on the show. However, it only intends to publish "a summary of findings", rather than the full report.

Channel 4's chief executive previously said the review was due back in the summer, but it has not yet been published.

Speaking to MPs earlier this week, Ofcom boss Dame Melanie Dawes said the report was due back "any day now".

BBC News has approached Channel 4 for a response.

Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, have previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading.

If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

articles.title: Two named storms in two days as Austen and Boelo target UK
articles.summary: The Met Office has named a new storm, Boelo, which is set to bring another round of stormy weather to the UK over the weekend.
articles.body:
The Met Office have named a new storm, Boelo, which is set to bring another round of stormy weather to the UK over the weekend.

Storm Boelo will be hot on the heels of Storm Austen, the first named storm of the season.

Storm Austen is expected to bring strong winds to south-west England during Friday morning.

The Met Office has issued an amber wind warning for Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly, Plymouth and parts of Devon valid between 1am and 10am on Friday.

Gusts of wind will widely reach 60-70mph, and perhaps 80mph in exposed locations.

Winds of this strength will blow some trees over, bringing a significant risk of transport disruption and there may also be some power cuts.

Some buildings could potentially be damaged by the strongest winds, leading to a risk of flying debris at the height of the storm.

Yellow wind warnings cover most of England and Wales with gusts of wind on Friday forecast to reach 45-60mph, with 70mph gusts likely in some places.

As strong as these winds are, the most damaging winds will run to the south of the low pressure centre.

That puts north-west France firmly in the firing line and parts of Brittany could see gusts close to 90mph.

The Channel Islands are also expecting severe gales with gusts up to 80mph.

All schools have been told to close on Friday because of the high winds predicted to be caused by Storm Austen, the Government of Jersey has said.

Heavy rain in Scotland may cause some localised flooding with a Met Office yellow warning for 20-40mm of rain forecast with up to 80mm accumulating in a few areas through Friday.

Storm Boelo to bring travel disruption over the weekend

Storm Boelo will bring wet and windy weather across the whole of the UK on Saturday with poor travelling conditions expected due to surface water and spray on faster roads and motorways.

The strongest winds will move into Scotland on Saturday afternoon, reaching a peak overnight.

The Met Office have also issued yellow wind warnings for Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England valid on Saturday and lasting most of Sunday.

Gusts are forecast to reach 50-65mph widely and could reach 80mph in exposed locations.

There could be some localised disruption with strong winds funnelling through the Central Lowlands for a time.

Transport disruption is expected and there may be some power cuts. Following recent spells of wet weather, there is an additional risk of some localised flooding.

Is it unusual to see two storms so close together?

It's not unusual to get storms so close together, in fact they quite often arrive in clusters.

A strong jet stream is needed to rapidly develop powerful wind storms. The process involved in creating such storms involves shifting warmer air northwards and cooler air southwards across vast areas of the Atlantic.

These temperature contrasts can provide a fertile environment for new low pressure systems to develop and if these subsequently get steered beneath a developmental area of a powerful jet stream, they can rapidly develop to create a new named storm with damaging winds.

Is there a hosepipe ban in my area? What you need to know

Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer.

The only month with no named storms in the eleven years that we've been naming storms in the UK, is May.

The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months.

This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year.

In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November.

articles.title: Meet Chaz, the 13-year-old who turned his birthday into a charity tradition despite a painful herniated disc, raising $4,000 in 2025
articles.summary: Thirteen-year-old Charlie “Chaz” turned his birthday into an opportunity to help others, organising an annual 5K fundraiser that raised $4,000 in 2025.
articles.body: Thirteen-year-old Charlie “Chaz” turned his birthday into an opportunity to help others, organising an annual 5K fundraiser that raised $4,000 in 2025. For the fourth consecutive year, Chaz brought together family, friends and community supporters to raise money for children with brain tumours and a cause close to his family. The young fundraiser raised $3,000 for the Pediatric Brain Tumor Foundation (PBTF) and another $1,000 to support awareness of neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC), a disease affecting a member of his family. What made the event particularly remarkable was that Chaz was dealing with a painful herniated disc that caused leg weakness in the weeks leading up to the run. Despite the setback, he chose to walk the 5K rather than cancel it.A birthday tradition built around giving backChaz's annual 5K has grown into a family and community tradition, bringing together people who want to support children affected by brain tumours. In 2025, he organised the event for the fourth year in a row, using his birthday as an opportunity to raise funds and awareness for causes that matter to him.The fundraiser generated $3,000 for PBTF, which supports childhood brain tumour research and provides resources for affected families. Chaz also raised $1,000 for neuroendocrine carcinoma awareness, a cause that holds personal significance because a member of his family is battling the disease.His mother said Chaz has long had a passion for helping others. Even as he faced his own health challenges, she said, he never considered cancelling the event.A herniated disc did not stop him from taking partIn the weeks before the 2025 event, Chaz developed a herniated disc that caused significant pain and weakness in his legs. His condition required an MRI at midnight and extensive physical therapy.Despite the discomfort, Chaz remained committed to the fundraiser. Rather than running the course, he walked the 5K alongside friends while other participants ran.His decision allowed him to continue the birthday tradition while adapting to his physical limitations. The experience became a defining part of his 2025 fundraiser, demonstrating his determination to support the causes he had chosen even when participating was more difficult than expected.His fundraising efforts extended beyond the 5KChaz continued supporting the Pediatric Brain Tumor Foundation after his birthday event. In November 2025, he joined PBTF and the Boston Celtics for the “Move4Heather” event, rallying friends to participate in a 50/50 auction.During the holiday season, he also organised a grocery gift-card drive for families in need. Donors received special gift bags containing holiday fudge and other treats supplied by local bakers and sponsors.Chaz set himself a goal of carrying out charitable acts in his community every month, extending his efforts beyond a single annual event. He has been supported by a group known as the “Chaz Bus Crew”, which has accompanied him in his charitable activities.The causes behind his fundraiserThe Pediatric Brain Tumor Foundation is a US non-profit organisation that supports childhood brain tumour research, provides resources for affected families and advocates for policies to improve care for young patients. The foundation says its work is aimed at advancing research and helping families navigate the challenges that follow a child's diagnosis.Neuroendocrine carcinoma is a rare and aggressive form of cancer that develops from neuroendocrine cells. Chaz's decision to raise money for awareness of the disease reflects its personal significance to his family, although the foundation's profile does not identify the relative affected.By supporting both causes, Chaz used his birthday fundraiser to direct attention and donations towards childhood brain tumours and a separate disease affecting someone close to him.A young fundraiser determined to keep helpingChaz's 2025 fundraiser combined a personal milestone with community support for two causes. The $4,000 raised was divided between PBTF and neuroendocrine carcinoma awareness, while his decision to walk the 5K allowed him to continue the event despite his injury.His efforts also continued through the “Move4Heather” event and the holiday gift-card drive, reflecting his goal of making charitable acts part of his routine throughout the year.Through an annual birthday 5K and other community initiatives, Chaz has shown how a young person can bring family, friends and supporters together to help others.You use AI every day. articles.title: El Salvador's president threatens Haitian gangs over military hostages
articles.summary: Four members of the so-called Gang Suppression Force have been missing since Sunday.
articles.body:
El Salvador's president has said he has launched a military operation to rescue four air force personnel who have been missing in Haiti since Sunday.

Threatening further action, Nayib Bukele said that Wednesday's attack was "nothing" compared with what would happen if all the hostages - who he said were not combatants - were not returned alive.

They went missing after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups," El Salvador's armed forces said. The ambush occurred in Croix-des-Bouquets, an area controlled by armed groups.

They were part of the so-called Gang Suppression Force (GSF), approved by the United Nations Security Council earlier this month, to tackle escalating gang violence in Haiti.

According to an X post from Bukele, the mission consisted of pilots and technical personnel, whose primary jobs were to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".

His post said the Salvadoran military operation's single objective was to bring the four men back home alive.

He added that if all four were returned alive, without being harmed, "everything will go back to how it was before the kidnapping".

Bukele added they were kidnapped "in a cowardly manner" while returning after buying food at a market in the area.

A statement released by the Armed Forces of El Salvador on Sunday said the group was ambushed while travelling back to its camp in an armoured vehicle, which caught fire after being hit by explosives.

So far, no gang has claimed responsibility for the attack.

Salvadoran helicopters were deployed to assist, with multiple attempts to make an approach by land and air hampered by fighting and local security conditions, the armed forces said.

On Wednesday, before Bukele announced the launch of the military operation, the GSF said it was searching for the four missing personnel following the attack.

It added that it had "engaged armed gang elements, with helicopter support" and that early reports had indicated that several gang members were killed.

Earlier this week, the UN warned that Haiti's armed gangs were adapting to intensified security conditions, saying that they were "stepping up reprisals against civilians and extending their reach into rural areas".

Haiti has not held elections since 2016, and two weeks ago postponed presidential and legislative elections - scheduled for 13 December - indefinitely.

The country has been wracked by economic chaos, a political vacuum and increasingly violent gang warfare since its president was assassinated in 2021.

More than 5,500 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti in 2024. Armed gangs currently control about 85% of the capital, Port-au-Prince.

articles.title: In North Carolina, a town sued a couple accused of feeding vulture swarms; neighbours say the birds have damaged roofs and created sanitation problems
articles.summary: A residential street in Hillsborough has become the setting for an unusual legal fight, with local officials taking a couple to court over dozens of
articles.body: A residential street in Hillsborough has become the setting for an unusual legal fight, with local officials taking a couple to court over dozens of vultures that residents say gather near their home. The case pits neighbours who want the birds gone against two residents who say they are being blamed unfairly. At stake is a practical question, how far does a person's responsibility extend when wild animals settle near a house? What follows sets out the accusations, the defence, the rule changes the town has already made, and what remains undecided as the dispute moves forward through the courts.Queen Street neighbours describe years of vulture trouble, from loosened roof tiles to droppingsResidents of Queen Street say the problem has persisted for years. Holden Richards told ABC11 that the birds unsettle him and that he does not consider them good neighbours. He said they mark their territory with droppings and have long, sharp talons, which makes them unwelcome on a roof. Richards watched vultures pull tiles off a neighbour's house, and tiles later came off his own roof and landed in his garden, which he believes was the birds' doing. He had to pay for the repair. He also believes almost every household nearby has complained to the town. Photographs submitted to the court show vultures circling a house that Richards believes belongs to Ken and Linda Ostrand.Hillsborough town officials accuse the couple of feeding vultures and seek a court injunctionThe town has filed a complaint against the Ostrands, alleging that they fed scraps to the vultures and even gave some of the birds names. Officials are asking for an injunction to stop the alleged feeding, which they say has created a safety concern. Following the first complaints, the town also changed its ordinance to restrict the feeding of wildlife beyond traditional bird feeders. Linda Ostrand told ABC11 that the new rule means nobody in town may throw seed on the ground, and that feeders must hang five feet off the ground.Linda Ostrand disputes the accusations, saying the vultures were present before she moved inIn a response filed with the court, the couple denied feeding the vultures. They argued that the presence of birds proves nothing about who attracted them, comparing it to assuming that anyone wearing tennis shoes must be a Wimbledon player. Linda Ostrand says she is being singled out. She called the lawsuit ridiculous but accepted that officials must respond when somebody complains. A longtime wildlife rescuer, she also defended the role vultures play in the ecosystem. Without them, she said, people would loudly protest about animals killed on roads, because the birds act as natural waste disposers.Court date still unscheduled as town officials decline to comment while the litigation continuesNo court date has been set for the civil case in Orange County, so the outcome remains uncertain for neighbours, town officials and the Ostrands alike. Town officials have declined to comment while the litigation is ongoing. Linda Ostrand said she does not know what she is supposed to do, and asked whether she should simply tell the vultures that the street is a no-feeding zone.You use AI every day. articles.title: Oregon woman was diagnosed with triple-negative breast cancer, then her husband's 300-member gaming community raised $1 million for research
articles.summary: Gaming isn't always just about passing the time by pressing some buttons; the people who share your likes and hobbies often end up becoming a part of a
articles.body: Gaming isn't always just about passing the time by pressing some buttons; the people who share your likes and hobbies often end up becoming a part of a community that takes the form of friendship, one that is bonded in happiness and sadness, both. When Jessica's life was threatened by breast cancer, her husband's gaming community with 300 members came to her rescue. They rallied around the couple and raised more than $1 million for lifesaving research, as per a report by Woman's World.A devastating diagnosisWhen Oregon couple Jessica and her husband Matt Conwell were led into a consulting room, Matt spotted a box of tissues. "Bad news," he predicted, and it was. Jessica had triple-negative breast cancer. Stressed and shocked by the news, the couple began their research but the more they read, the bleaker the future looked. “We’ll get through this together, as we always do,” Matt promised.Jessica and Matt met when they attended the same graduate school, where Jessica was working on her PhD in psychology and Matt on his M.B.A. They married in ’98, and Jessica started a private practice, while Matt turned a school project into the Portland Local Area Network (PDXLAN), centred on his video gaming community.Matt hosted huge game-a-thon parties where 300 or more gamers battled one another from Thursday to Sunday evening, with late-night sleep breaks to recharge. Jessica was always there helping out, which led to her nickname "conference mom."After learning the news of her diagnosis, the community was devastated. Jessica's treatment was also gruelling: a double mastectomy, chemo and radiation. She lost her hair and a quarter of her body weight. Her mood bounced from hopeful to bleak, and so did Matt’s. But he tried hard to be Jessica’s rock.Rallying behind a friendFor the past several years, the gamers had raised money for charities that support sick children and people experiencing homelessness. Now, they wanted to redirect their generosity. “You told us the new drugs are helping, so this session, we want to raise money to support more research,” the group announced to Matt.The very next LAN party, a screen displayed a digital tote board that ticked up with each new donation. Matt fought back tears as the numbers rose to a record $55,000. The gamers' support carried Matt through Jessica's bout of sepsis, but she began a steady recovery. When she returned to the next game-a-thon, members surrounded her with cheers and hugs.So far, the PDXLAN contributions have topped $1 million for cancer research. Meanwhile, Jessica has been cancer-free for five years. “I never knew how many people were in my corner,” she says. “I was never alone.” Matt agreed. “New treatments saved Jessica, but there’s still so much to be done. Maybe our contributions will help a scientist make that next life-saving breakthrough!”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2020, a Minnesota couple bought a home reached through a neighbour's gravel driveway; a feud over trees and a security camera led to $27,000 in damages, but an appeals court reversed the $20,000 privacy award
articles.summary: A dispute between two Minnesota couples over a shared driveway, tree removal and a security camera has taken another turn after an appeals court reversed
articles.body: A dispute between two Minnesota couples over a shared driveway, tree removal and a security camera has taken another turn after an appeals court reversed a $20,000 privacy award. On October 19, 2026, the Minnesota Court of Appeals reversed part of a $27,000 damages judgment in Leonard Ruby v. Dominic Stahley. According to the court’s opinion, published by Justia, the conflict began after Dominic and Melissa Stahley bought a neighbouring property in 2020 that could only be accessed through a gravel driveway on Leonard and Sandra Ruby’s land. The court sent the privacy claim back for further proceedings while reducing damages for unlawful tree removal.A shared driveway sparks a neighbourhood feudThe Rubys bought their property in Forest Lake, Minnesota, in 2014. Four years later, the Stahleys purchased the neighbouring property, whose only access to a public road was through a gravel driveway crossing the Rubys’ land. A written easement agreement from 2014 allowed the Stahleys to use the driveway but required them to seek written permission before undertaking maintenance. It also prohibited removing trees from the easement area without the Rubys’ written consent.In 2020, the Stahleys notified their neighbours that they intended to mow grass, clear brush, trim branches, remove trees and repair the driveway. The Rubys permitted snow removal but refused permission for the other work. The Stahleys nevertheless carried out maintenance activities between 2020 and 2024, worsening the dispute.Security camera leads to a privacy lawsuitThe neighbours also accused each other of inappropriate behaviour. Melissa Stahley alleged that the Rubys intimidated the family, verbally abused them and obstructed their access to the property. Dominic Stahley installed a motion-activated camera on another neighbour’s property, with the owner’s permission, to document the alleged conduct.In January 2024, the Rubys sued the Stahleys for breach of the easement agreement, trespass, unlawful tree removal and intrusion upon seclusion, a legal claim involving invasion of privacy. The Stahleys filed counterclaims for trespass, quiet title and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The district court ruled in the Rubys’ favour on their claims and dismissed the counterclaims. Following a damages trial in June 2025, it awarded the Rubys $27,000: $20,000 for invasion of privacy, $6,000 in trebled nominal damages for unlawful tree removal and $1,000 for breach of the easement agreement and trespass.Appeals court reverses the $20,000 awardThe Stahleys challenged the privacy ruling, arguing that the evidence did not establish an unlawful intrusion. The appeals court agreed that the claim required further consideration. To establish intrusion upon seclusion, a claimant must show an intentional intrusion that is highly offensive and concerns a matter in which there is a legitimate expectation of privacy. The court examined images captured by the camera. They showed the shared driveway, vehicles parked on the Rubys’ property, Leonard Ruby clearing snow and the outline of the home behind trees. However, the evidence did not show that the camera was aimed directly at the home’s windows or could record its interior.The court noted that the area captured was visible to people lawfully using the driveway. It concluded that reasonable people could differ on whether the camera constituted a highly offensive intrusion into a private area. Therefore, the district court should not have decided the privacy claim through summary judgment. The appeals court reversed the finding of liability and the $20,000 award, remanding the matter for further proceedings. This does not mean the camera was definitively found lawful; the privacy claim remains unresolved.Tree damages reduced, other claims rejectedThe appeals court also ruled that the district court had incorrectly tripled the $2,000 in nominal damages awarded for unlawful tree removal, producing a $6,000 award. Under Minnesota law, treble damages for unlawfully cutting or damaging trees must be calculated from actual damages, rather than nominal damages awarded when the precise financial loss has not been established. The court therefore reduced this award to $2,000.It upheld the district court’s decision to award nominal rather than actual damages for the property-related claims, finding no abuse of discretion. It also affirmed the dismissal of the Stahleys’ counterclaims, concluding that the evidence did not establish the extreme and outrageous conduct required for an emotional-distress claim or sufficient grounds for their other claims.The ruling leaves the privacy dispute open while clarifying that tree-related damages cannot be tripled without proof of actual loss. It also underscores how disagreements over shared access, property maintenance and surveillance can become complicated legal battles when neighbours dispute both their rights and the boundaries of their properties.You use AI every day. articles.title: Indian-origin man, 24, killed in Canada highway crash days after permanent residency approval
articles.summary: Jaskeerat Singh Naukhria, a 24-year-old Indian-origin man, tragically died in a highway crash in British Columbia, just days after receiving his permanent residency approval. Three others were injured, with two in critical condition. An online fundraiser has been launched to support his family.
articles.body: An Indian-origin man was killed in a head-on collision on a highway in British Columbia, Canada, while three others travelling with him were injured, two of them critically. The crash occurred on Saturday near Merritt.The deceased was identified as Jaskeerat Singh Naukhria, 24, who moved to Canada in 2024. A GoFundMe representative said Naukhria had received approval for his permanent residency last week, according to Canadian media reports.Naukhria was driving a white Toyota RAV4 on Highway 5, also known as the Coquihalla Highway, when a black Toyota Tacoma entered the highway near Lac Le Jeune and collided with his vehicle, witnesses told police.Police said they had received multiple complaints about a vehicle travelling southbound in the northbound lanes before the crash. Officers responded to the incident at around 8.30 am.The three passengers travelling with Naukhria were taken to hospital. Two were reported to be in critical condition. All four people in the RAV4 were aged between 24 and 38.The pickup truck’s 22-year-old driver, a resident of Coldwater, was its only occupant. He suffered minor injuries and was detained on suspicion of impaired driving, police said.An online fundraiser has been launched in Naukhria’s name, with a target of $100,000 to help cover funeral and memorial expenses, related costs and financial support for his family.“The sudden passing of Jaskeerat has left our family, friends, and everyone who knew him heartbroken,” the fundraiser page states.You use AI every day.
