articles.title: A Yorkshire couple built a four-bedroom home using straw bales and lime plaster; completed in 2018, the energy-conscious property is now listed for £2.75 million
articles.summary: A four-bedroom country house in North Yorkshire, built using straw bales and lime plaster, has come onto the property market with a guide price of £2.75
articles.body: A four-bedroom country house in North Yorkshire, built using straw bales and lime plaster, has come onto the property market with a guide price of £2.75 million. Known as The Lime House, the property in Whenby was built by Jonathan and Sara Banister and completed in 2018, replacing a 1960s bungalow on the site. Inspired by a conversation with Grand Designs presenter Kevin McCloud about sustainable construction, the couple pursued an unconventional building approach while retaining the appearance of a traditional English farmhouse. The 4,338-square-foot home combines natural building materials with modern features such as solar panels, triple glazing, underfloor heating and mechanical ventilation with heat recovery. Set within approximately 4.5 acres, the property also includes landscaped gardens, a natural pond and additional outbuildings.How straw bales and lime plaster shaped the houseThe Lime House was designed as a self-build project, with architectural support from Native Architects. The couple replaced the existing bungalow with a home that used straw bales as an insulating material and lime-based finishes for the walls.Straw-bale construction involves using compacted straw within a building's wall system. When properly designed and protected from persistent moisture, the material can provide effective insulation. Lime plaster and render offer a breathable finish that allows moisture vapour to move through the wall assembly.The project also involved specialist straw-bale building courses run by Straw Works, helping the owners develop the skills and confidence required for the construction process. The house was completed in 2018 after nearly two years of work.Despite the use of unconventional materials, the finished property has the appearance of an established country home, with traditional masonry details and carefully chosen natural finishes.Energy-conscious features inside the £2.75 million propertyThe house incorporates several technologies intended to improve energy efficiency and indoor comfort. These include solar panels, triple-glazed windows, underfloor heating and a mechanical ventilation system with heat recovery.The ventilation system exchanges stale indoor air for fresh air while recovering heat from the outgoing air, helping reduce heat loss. Triple glazing limits heat transfer through windows, while underfloor heating distributes warmth across the living spaces.The property also features rainwater harvesting and passive infrared lighting. Together with the insulated walls, these elements form part of the house's energy-conscious design.However, the presence of these systems does not, by itself, establish the home's annual energy consumption or running costs. Those figures would depend on factors such as household use, weather conditions and system performance.Four bedrooms, four bathrooms and spacious living areasThe Lime House measures approximately 4,338 square feet, or 403 square metres, and is arranged over two-and-a-half floors, including a mezzanine. Its four double bedrooms each have an en-suite bathroom.The interior includes two reception rooms and a large open-plan kitchen, dining and living area. A stone staircase, substantial fireplace, wooden panelling, handmade bricks and stonework contribute to the traditional country-house character.The design combines open communal spaces with separate rooms, allowing the property to accommodate family life and entertaining. The use of natural finishes carries through much of the interior, complementing the materials used in the building's construction.Gardens, a natural pond and additional buildingsThe property occupies approximately 4.5 acres and includes landscaped gardens and outdoor entertaining areas. A rain-fed natural pond forms part of the grounds and is intended to support local wildlife.Additional buildings include a barn and a studio or workshop, providing space for hobbies, creative work or other uses. Their precise permitted uses would depend on the property's planning and building regulations.The setting offers views of the surrounding North Yorkshire countryside, combining the privacy of a rural property with the facilities of a substantial modern home.Kevin McCloud's influence on the projectMcCloud, the presenter of the television series Grand Designs, is known for featuring self-build projects and exploring alternative approaches to architecture and design. According to Country Life, a conversation with him about sustainable construction helped inspire the Banisters to consider materials such as straw bales and lime plaster.McCloud's role was inspirational rather than that of the house's architect. Native Architects provided professional architectural support for the project, helping the couple navigate the design and construction process.The result demonstrates how natural building materials can be incorporated into a contemporary home without abandoning the traditional appearance associated with English country houses.An unconventional home on the property marketThe Lime House is being marketed by Savills with a guide price of £2.75 million. Its appeal rests on a combination of rural land, generous living space, traditional styling and an approach to construction that differs from that of many conventional houses.The property has also featured in the revised edition of The Buildings of England: Yorkshire, part of the architectural guide series founded by Nikolaus Pevsner.Completed in 2018, the house brings together straw-bale insulation, lime finishes and modern energy-conscious systems in a design intended to balance comfort, character and environmental considerations. Its current listing places that approach within the luxury country-house market.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: First human case of Shamonda virus detected in France, officials say
articles.summary: The disease, which usually affects cattle, has been identified in a patient who died in early October.
articles.body:
The first known human case of the Shamonda virus (Shav) has been detected in a patient who died in early October, French authorities have said.

Health officials said it was an "exceptional case in a severely immunocompromised patient" and there was currently no risk to the public.

Shav is a disease that primarily affects cattle and can be spread by infected midges. Cases have also occurred in sheep, goats, alpacas and horses, but infections in people were previously unheard of.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said it was monitoring the situation and officials were still investigating how the virus had spread to a human.

It is currently thought the patient contracted Shav through a midge bite in eastern France, the country's health and agriculture ministries said on Thursday, where cases were first identified in animals in the spring.

They said the patient was being treated for a serious illness in a Lyon hospital and experienced neurological complications thought to have been "very likely linked" to the virus, based on initial findings.

The statement stressed that their immune system was weakened, leaving them more vulnerable to getting ill.

"Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered non-transmissible to humans," it noted, having only been identified in animals "despite decades of circulation of the Shamonda virus in Africa and Asia".

Dairy herds that catch Shav from bites can experience fever, diarrhoea and poor milk production.

The ECDC said it was working with French and European partners to investigate the "potential public health implications" of the infection.

The first cases of the virus in Europe were identified in late July, the agency said. It has since been detected in farm animals in several countries, including Ireland, Germany, Italy and Spain, as well as in Jersey.

The case has also been reported to the World Health Organization.

articles.title: Did strategic mistrust prompt Germany to pull out of Boeing's Ghost Bat deal
articles.summary: Germany has told Boeing that it will not directly buy the company's MQ-28 Ghost Bat drone wingman, as Berlin readjusts its plans for a Collaborative
articles.body: Germany has told Boeing that it will not directly buy the company's MQ-28 Ghost Bat drone wingman, as Berlin readjusts its plans for a Collaborative Combat Aircraft programme. A Boeing spokesperson said the German ministry of defence had informed the company of the decision but did not give details as to why.The ministry on its part said it does not give information on potential projects, citing procurement and public contracting law and the requirement that such matters first go to parliament.The decision comes as Germany moves ahead with plans to acquire F-35 fighter jets from the US, despite initial resistance to the purchase. However, Berlin appears to be taking a more cautious approach to its next-generation uncrewed combat aircraft.Designed to fly alongside crewed fighter jets and carry out strike missions, these drone wingmen are intended to extend the reach and combat capabilities of conventional aircraft while reducing risks to pilots. Germany had aimed to field the capability by 2029, potentially making it the first European country to do so. That timeline, however, now appears uncertain. Berlin is expected to defer the introduction of the capability until the early 2030s, with flight testing scheduled to begin in 2027. This would give Boeing and other contenders an opportunity to compete for the programme.Several companies are positioning themselves as alternatives. Germany's Helsing is pitching its CA-1 Europa, which the company says will be ready for operations by 2029. A partnership between Airbus and US firm Kratos is offering the U740 Valkyrie. The companies announced its first flight on Monday and said they remained on track to deliver a combat-ready uncrewed aircraft by 2029. General Atomics Aeronautical Systems could also offer a platform from its Gambit family. A company spokesperson said it had held repeated discussions with Germany about its offering.The strategic cost of buying foreign weaponsGermany's decision comes amid a broader debate over how defence procurement intersects with diplomacy, national security and strategic autonomy. Governments must weigh the advantages of acquiring advanced foreign weapons against the risks of becoming dependent on overseas suppliers. Recent debates surrounding the US-led F-35 programme illustrate how political disagreements and export restrictions can affect access to military technology.A weapons purchase involves far more than the initial acquisition of hardware. Buyers often depend on suppliers for spare parts, software updates, ammunition, maintenance and upgrades throughout a platform’s service life. Export approvals, sanctions and restrictions on technology transfers can also determine how freely a country can operate, modify or upgrade its equipment.Turkey’s removal from the F-35 programme in July 2019 remains one of the clearest examples of these risks.Ankara was an original partner in the programme but proceeded with its purchase of Russia’s S-400 air defence system despite Washington’s objections. The US argued that operating the Russian system alongside the F-35 could expose sensitive information about the fighter’s capabilities. Turkey subsequently lost its planned F-35 deliveries as well as its role in the programme’s industrial supply chain.European countries have acquired the F-35 for its stealth capabilities, advanced sensors and interoperability with allied forces. European companies also participate in its manufacturing and support networks. However, participation in the programme does not give buyers complete control over the aircraft’s development or upgrades.Britain’s efforts to integrate additional weapons onto the F-35, for instance, depend on software updates managed through the US-led programme. Delays can therefore disrupt national plans to introduce new capabilities. Meanwhile, claims that the F-35 has a remote kill switch have not been substantiated. On October 8, Reuters reported that Portugal was seriously considering the F-35, alongside European alternatives, to replace its F-16 fleet.The implications for IndiaFor India, these questions are closely linked to its long-standing pursuit of strategic autonomy. New Delhi sources military equipment from Russia, the United States, France, Israel and other countries while seeking to expand domestic manufacturing and access to advanced technology.India operates several American-origin platforms, including C-17 and C-130J transport aircraft, P-8I maritime patrol aircraft, Apache attack helicopters, Chinook heavy-lift helicopters, MH-60R naval helicopters and M777 howitzers. Defence cooperation with Washington has also expanded to include proposals for co-production and technology transfer.However, the history of US sanctions against India underscores the potential risks of geopolitical differences. Sanctions followed India’s 1998 nuclear tests, while the possibility of punitive measures under the US Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA) became a concern after New Delhi purchased Russia’s S-400 air defence system.India's circumstances differ significantly from Turkey’s, nevertheless, they highlight a common challenge: advanced military equipment can deepen a country’s dependence on the supplier for critical technology, maintenance and future upgrades.New Delhi has sought to manage that risk by diversifying its sources of military hardware, strengthening domestic production and pressing for technology transfer. The broader lesson from Germany’s reassessment of its drone-wingman programme and the disputes surrounding the F-35 is that defence procurement is not simply a question of which weapon offers the best performance. It is also about who controls the technology, who can restrict its use and how much strategic freedom the buyer retains over the life of the system.

articles.title: Russia to review Trump’s invitation to Putin for G20 summit, possible talks on Ukraine
articles.summary: Russia will review the US invitation for President Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit in Miami in December, but no decision has been taken yet,
articles.body: Russia will review the US invitation for President Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit in Miami in December, but no decision has been taken yet, Kremlin spokesman said on Thursday.Spokesman Dmitry Peskov also said that Moscow viewed the growing involvement of European countries in efforts to reach a peace settlement in Ukraine as a positive development. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept,” he said.Putin has not attended an in-person G20 summit since 2019, although he participated virtually in a leaders' meeting when India hosted the summit in November 2023.The G20 brings together major advanced and emerging economies, including the United States, China, India, the United Kingdom and members of the European Union.The meeting is scheduled to take place at the Trump National Doral golf club, and may include talks to end the Ukraine war.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week that Washington was working to arrange a trilateral meeting involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States to discuss peace negotiations.He said Kyiv was ready to participate in meetings anywhere and in any format.Zelenskyy also suggested that the G20 summit in the United States could provide an opportunity for the meeting, although he said no agreement had been confirmed by either Moscow or Washington.“Another possibility is for the meeting to take place in the United States during the G20 summit. articles.title: Chhattisgarh IPS officer Ankita Sharma gets show-cause notice after AK-47 firing video goes viral
articles.summary: RAIPUR: Chhattisgarh Police Headquarters on Thursday issued a show-cause notice to senior IPS officer Ankita Sharma after a video showing her firing an
articles.body: RAIPUR: Chhattisgarh Police Headquarters on Thursday issued a show-cause notice to senior IPS officer Ankita Sharma after a video showing her firing an AK-47 rifle into the air during a traditional weapon-worship ritual on Dussehra in Rajnandgaon went viral.The incident involving Rajnandgaon superintendent of police (SP) Sharma has triggered a debate over safety, discipline and weapon-handling protocols.The video showed Sharma, dressed in a saree, firing several rounds from an AK-47 after the weapon-worship ritual, news agency PTI reported.Rajnandgaon Range inspector general of police Ajay Yadav said Sharma fired the rifle after the traditional 'Shastra Puja' at Police Lines on October 20, on the occasion of Vijayadashami.The police headquarters took serious cognisance of the matter, finding that the act was not in accordance with police weapon-handling rules. It has sought an explanation from Sharma, Yadav said.He added that the headquarters had sought clarification over the apparent disregard for safety protocols, as negative comments on the viral video were damaging the dignity of the police force, PTI reported."After receiving the SP's reply, I will record my observations and forward the matter to the police headquarters. Further action will be taken in accordance with the directions received from there," the IG said.While some social media users defended Sharma, arguing that she was following a tradition, others criticised her handling of the weapon.Retired IPS officer RK Vij told PTI that firing should be carried out only at a safe location and with adequate precautions."The tradition is essentially about performing the worship of weapons, not firing them. Such firing carries the risk of accidents and should be avoided," Vij said.An IPS officer, requesting anonymity, said firing blank rounds, commonly known as 'awazi kartoos', was part of the Shastra Puja tradition followed across the state. Live ammunition was not used on such occasions, the officer added, PTI reported.The officer also pointed out that even a bullet fired into the air comes back down and can injure people nearby.Former Indian Army officer KJS Dhillon also raised concerns on social media over the weapon-handling practices seen in the videos, saying safety precautions had been violated."Dangerously incorrect handling of a loaded weapon - All aspects of safety of weapon handling violated - Pointing a loaded weapon in all directions. Ppl (people) in background are visibly terrified - Firing a service weapon for an unauthorised act in a non-authorised dress - Basic weapon handling drill taught in the...academies not adhered to - Such irresponsible action can cause death or hurt to self or others...," he wrote.Another social media user, identifying himself as Army veteran Colonel Deepak Kumar, described the act as reckless and unprofessional and questioned Sharma's handling of the rifle after firing.Some users suggested that only blank ammunition should be used for ceremonial firing, PTI reported.Others defended Sharma, arguing that the incident should not overshadow her professional record.A social media user identifying himself as 'former Major LS Choudhary' acknowledged shortcomings in weapon handling but said they should be corrected without discrediting her work in Chhattisgarh.Another user, Narendra Negi, defended Sharma, saying she was a trained IPS officer.He contended that some of the criticism stemmed from her firing the rifle while wearing a saree.Rajnandgaon Additional Superintendent of Police Kirtan Rathore was also seen firing an AK-47 after Sharma in another video.Videos showing police personnel firing weapons after the ritual in other districts, including Raipur, Bilaspur, Raigarh, Durg, Kabirdham and Bastar, were also shared with the media on Tuesday.(With agnecy inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Raipur | Silver Rate in Raipur | Bank Holidays in Raipur | Public Holidays in Raipur | Raipur AQI | Weather in Raipur | Petrol Price in Raipur | Diesel Price in Raipur | CNG Price in Raipur | LPG Price in RaipurStay updated with the latest Raipur news. articles.title: PTR on high alert against owl poaching ahead of Diwali
articles.summary: Palamu Tiger Reserve increases vigilance ahead of Diwali to curb owl poaching, with intensified check-post inspections and strict enforcement of wildlife laws.
articles.body: Daltonganj: With Diwali approaching, the Palamu Tiger Reserve (PTR) has stepped up surveillance across its forest divisions to prevent the trapping and hunting of owls, which become particularly vulnerable during the festive season due to superstition-linked demand.Forest officials said owls are often targeted ahead of Diwali because they are associated with goddess Lakshmi and are believed by some to bring wealth and prosperity. The birds are also sought for occult and tantric rituals, with body parts such as bones, claws, skulls, feathers and meat reportedly used in talismans.“We are alert to the threat faced by owls during this period. Forest guards and trackers have been instructed to maintain strict vigilance,” said Kumar Ashish, deputy director, south division, PTR.Officials said special attention is being paid to people carrying slingshots, a commonly used tool for hunting or injuring birds. Personnel deployed at PTR’s eight check posts in the south division are conducting intensified inspections of visitors, cyclists and their belongings.The check posts are located at Garu, Rud, Vijaypur, Netarhat, Sohar, Aksi, Bareysanr and Maromar.“Owls are protected under the Wildlife Protection Act. Hunting, poaching or trading in owls is a punishable offence,” a forest official said.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Irish government minister criticises rape crisis centre consent ad
articles.summary: Jim O'Callaghan described the video as "inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents".
articles.body:
The Irish minister for justice has criticised an advertisement produced by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) promoting consent, calling it "inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents".

The ad depicts two grandparents enthusiastically hugging a young boy, but when they approach their granddaughter she appears unhappy about the exchange.

It includes the message "not everyone wants a hug. Even from the people who love them".

The ad, which has since been removed, has attracted criticism and and also received international coverage in publications such as the New York Post.

Fianna Fáil politician Jim O'Callaghan, whose department funds the campaign, said the the video has since been removed following engagement with the DRCC.

He said the video "does not represent the views of the Government".

"It was both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents and has been removed by DRCC following my officials engagement with them.

"While it is vital to ensure that people understand the concept of consent when it comes to sexual relationships, this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive."

The video was part of a campaign titled 'We-Consent', which is led by the DRCC.

In a statement to Irish broadcaster RTÉ, the DRCC said: "We-Consent is a long-term campaign as part of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre's prevention work to increase the awareness and practice of consent in Ireland.

"We created three videos premised on the idea that boundaries should be respected from an early age and to respect others' boundaries too.

"We are going to remove the videos from our social media channels while we reflect on whether they are having the positive effect we want them to have."

As well as the Department of Justice, the 'We-Consent' campaign is also supported by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, and CUAN (the Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Agency).

All three have been approached for comment.

Fine Gael Senator Gareth Scahill said the video was a waste of resources.

"What's concerning here is public money has been used to fund an ad which at best has been ill-thought out, and at worst is offensive and potentially damaging to our older population," he said.

"The issue of consent is a very serious one and I acknowledge the important work the Rape Crisis Centre and other agencies do every day to advocate for all victims of rape and sexual violence, including children.

"But this publicly funded social media video is a million miles off the mark."

He added: "What's next? Will we need to sign consent forms at arrival halls in Dublin, Shannon, Knock and Cork airports this Christmas before we can greet family members?"

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said: "'We-Consent' is a programme created and developed by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, aimed at informing, educating, and engaging the public about all forms of consent.

"Social media videos shared recently as part of this programme were produced by DRCC at a low-cost using volunteers and are not part of a Government advertising campaign.

"The Department understands that DRCC intends to review these videos. They are being removed from their social media channels to enable this review."

articles.summary: A Minneapolis restaurant that experimented with eliminating prices and offering donation-based meals in protest against US Immigration and Customs
articles.body: A Minneapolis restaurant that experimented with eliminating prices and offering donation-based meals in protest against US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has announced it will shut down permanently by the end of 2026, Fox News reported.Modern Times Café, which rebranded as Post Modern Times earlier this year, had adopted a free and donation-based model in January, saying it would welcome everyone except ICE agents. Owner Dylan Alverson said he had spent the past six years trying to keep the business running but had exhausted all options without compromising its core principles.“For the last six years, I’ve been trying to prove that Modern Times can continue to exist,” Alverson wrote in a social media post on Saturday. He said he would spend the next two months celebrating the restaurant’s 16-year history and exploring ways to sustain similar businesses in the future.“The only way for places like Modern Times to exist in the future is to actively challenge the reasons why it can no longer exist,” he added.Restaurant adopted donation-based model amid ICE protestsIn January, Alverson announced that the restaurant would stop charging customers, saying he no longer wanted to generate money for a government he accused of harming citizens. The decision came amid heightened opposition to federal immigration enforcement operations in Minnesota, following the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.The restaurant operated without fixed prices for around six months before temporarily closing in July. When it reopened in August, it resumed charging customers but continued offering 25 free meals daily.Alverson told The New York Times in October that he was operating the restaurant with a “zero profit margin” and hoped its model could inspire other establishments. However, the arrangement placed considerable pressure on staff and reportedly resulted in customers waiting as long as two hours for meals, about half of which were provided free.Some neighbours also raised concerns that the offer could attract homeless people and those struggling with drug addiction.Speaking to Fox News Digital, Alverson stood by his earlier comments and pointed to the broader challenges facing independent restaurants.“I think a bigger question right now is how many independent restaurants are close to collapse?” he said.Alverson said he had spent years attempting to find a way to keep the business operating without abandoning its principles.
